doc.title: Nick Mondello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 19, 2022

title: Teaching beyond method books; lessons from Clark Terry and Paul Effman
summary: He writes silly-titled tunes instead of relying on method books, introduces why Parker and Gillespie matter, and credits Clark Terry and Paul Effman.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: So it’s a very, very, very deep point that over time, and this is one of the blessings about getting older, after a while you try things, they work, they don’t work, you bomb, and you get the kids. Another thing like that is I don’t primarily like to teach from the method books, okay? Now every student at some point in time when they’re in the school they’re going to get the Belwin Band Builder or the this or what-have-you. So there are concepts that I embellish or I take from the Belwin Band Builder let’s call it, or whatever it happens to be, and I write tunes for the kids, okay? And then of course you make silly names for the tunes like “Parade of the Peppy Pickled People” or something stupid like that, and it’s all about entertaining. Because we are entertainers by our nature. It’s innate, see? We happen to be teachers, and entertaining, encouraging, motivating and then being prepared for when failure happens, you know, with the kids. You know it’s something interesting, and I hope I’m not running on on this, but when you’re here, you know, teachers say, you know, “I asked this kid about Charlie Parker and you know he didn’t know anything about Charlie —” well the kid’s a sixth grader or seventh grader, whatever grader he happens to be. You know it’s our job to at least introduce not only who and what, when and where, but why — why Charlie Parker? Why Dizzy Gillespie and all — why the great vocalists you see? And getting them to buy into that, once they do, you know they say you know what? We trust this man or woman that’s teaching us, and apparently you know he must know his stuff or else they just grabbed him in from central casting. You know? Bring in a music teacher, here you go. But you know that’s a big, big, and I learned that, I’ll tell you where I learned that from. I learned that from Clark Terry. I learned that from one of the great music educators out there whose name © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

you may or may not know, Paul Effman. Okay? Paul, a music educator, came up with a model to have schools in — have music programs in private and parochial schools and eventually it developed into something like seven or eight hundred schools. But the idea was it’s entertaining and educational and motivating and something that you will always try to remember.
